results.summary: An additive commutative group of squarefree cardinality is additively cyclic.

results.title: Szele's criterion for cyclic numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Every group of order $n$ is cyclic if and only if $n$ is relatively prime to $\varphi(n)$, that is, $\gcd(n, \varphi(n)) = 1$, where $\varphi$ is Euler's totient function.

results.title: Bounded class for nilpotent Camina-type groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Kourovka Problem 17.47 (S. H. Ghate, A. S. Muktibodh) asks whether this proposition holds: there is a natural number $c$ such that every nilpotent group $G$ in which, for every $x \notin [G, G]$, the coset $x[G, G]$ of the commutator subgroup $[G, G]$ equals the conjugacy class $x^G$ of $x$, has nilpotency class at most $c$.

results.title: Nilpotent Camina-type groups have unbounded class
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is no natural number $c$ such that every nilpotent group $G$ in which, for every $x \notin [G, G]$, the coset $x[G, G]$ of the commutator subgroup $[G, G]$ equals the conjugacy class $x^G$ of $x$, has nilpotency class at most $c$. So Kourovka Problem 17.47 has a negative answer.

results.title: Local factor
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and natural numbers $p$ and $e$, the local factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent $e$ is $1$ if $e = 0$, $a(p)$ if $e = 1$, and $0$ if $e \ge 2$.

results.title: Coefficients for Entry 30
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(n) \in \mathbb{C}$ is $0$ when $n = 0$. When $n \ne 0$ it is the product, over the prime factors $p$ of $n$, of the local factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent the multiplicity of $p$ in $n$. The local factor at $p$ with exponent $e$ is $1$ for $e = 0$, $a(p)$ for $e = 1$, and $0$ for $e \ge 2$.

results.title: Terms of the Dirichlet series over non-squarefree integers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number $j$, put $n = j + 1$; the $j$-th term is $0$ if $n$ is squarefree and $n^{-s}$ otherwise. As $j$ ranges over the natural numbers, these are the terms of $\sum n^{-s}$ over non-squarefree $n \ge 1$.

results.title: Terms over squarefree integers with an odd number of prime factors
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number $j$, put $n = j + 1$; the $j$-th term is $n^{-s}$ if $n$ is squarefree and has an odd number of distinct prime factors, and $0$ otherwise. As $j$ ranges over the natural numbers, these are the terms of $\sum n^{-s}$ over squarefree $n \ge 1$ with an odd number of prime factors.

results.title: Signed multiplicative coefficient
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number $n$, let $a(p) = -p^{-s}$ for natural numbers $p$. The signed coefficient of $n$ is $0$ if $n = 0$ and, for $n \ne 0$, the product over the prime factors $p$ of $n$ of the local factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent the multiplicity of $p$ in $n$, where the local factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent $e$ is $1$ for $e = 0$, $a(p)$ for $e = 1$, and $0$ for $e \ge 2$.

results.title: Terms of the Dirichlet series over squarefree integers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a complex number $s$ and a natural number $j$, let $n = j + 1$; the $j$-th squarefree term is $n^{-s}$ if $n$ is squarefree and $0$ otherwise, so the series of these terms over $j \ge 0$ is $\sum n^{-s}$ over the squarefree $n \ge 1$.

results.title: Local factor at exponent zero
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural number $p$, the local factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent $0$ is $1$.

results.title: Local factor at exponent one
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural number $p$, the local factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent $1$ is $a(p)$.

results.title: Entry 30 local factors vanish at exponents at least two
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$, every $p \in \mathbb{N}$ and every $e \ge 2$, the Entry 30 local factor of $a$ at $p$ with exponent $e$ is $0$.

results.title: Entry 30 coefficients at squarefree integers
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every squarefree $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ne 0$, the Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(n)$ is the product of $a(p)$ over the prime factors $p$ of $n$.

results.title: Entry 30 coefficients vanish at nonzero non-squarefree natural numbers
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural number $n \ne 0$ that is not squarefree, the Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(n)$ is $0$.

results.title: Closed form of the Entry 30 coefficients
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ne 0$, the Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(n)$ equals the product of $a(p)$ over the prime factors $p$ of $n$ when $n$ is squarefree, and $c_a(n) = 0$ otherwise.

results.title: Summability of the Entry 30 coefficients
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and let $c > 1$ be real with $|a(p)| \le p^{-c}$ for every prime $p$. Then the Entry 30 coefficients $f_a(n)$ of $a$ (equal to $0$ at $n = 0$; for $n \ge 1$, the product of $a(p)$ over the primes $p \mid n$ if $n$ is squarefree, and $0$ otherwise) form a summable family over $n \ge 2$.

results.title: The Entry 30 coefficient at zero
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$, the Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(0)$ is $0$.

results.title: The Entry 30 coefficient at one
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$, the Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(1)$ is $1$.

results.title: Entry 30 coefficients at primes
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every prime $p$, the Entry 30 coefficient $c_a(p)$ equals $a(p)$.

results.title: Entry 30 coefficients vanish at higher prime powers
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$, every prime $p$ and every $e \ge 2$, the Entry 30 coefficient satisfies $c_a(p^e) = 0$.

results.title: Entry 30 coefficients are multiplicative
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every function $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and all coprime $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$, the Entry 30 coefficients $c_a$ satisfy $c_a(mn) = c_a(m)\,c_a(n)$.

results.title: Euler product for the Entry 30 coefficients
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and let $c > 1$ be real with $|a(p)| \le p^{-c}$ for every prime $p$. Write $f_a(n)$ for the Entry 30 coefficient of $a$ at $n$ (it is $0$ at $n = 0$; for $n \ge 1$ it is the product of $a(p)$ over the primes $p \mid n$ if $n$ is squarefree, and $0$ otherwise). Then the product of $1 + a(p)$ over all primes $p$ converges unconditionally to $1 + \sum_{n \ge 2} f_a(n)$.

results.title: Squarefree term, explicit form
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number $j$, the $j$-th term of the Dirichlet series over squarefree integers equals $(j + 1)^{-s}$ if $j + 1$ is squarefree and $0$ otherwise.

results.title: Summability of the squarefree terms
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every complex number $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the series of $n^{-s}$ over the squarefree $n \ge 1$ is summable.

results.title: Sum of $n^{-s}$ over squarefree $n$
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every complex number $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the sum of $n^{-s}$ over the squarefree $n \ge 1$ equals $\zeta(s)/\zeta(2s)$.

results.title: Odd-count squarefree term, explicit form
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For $s \in \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number $j$, the $j$-th term of the Dirichlet series over squarefree integers with an odd number of prime factors equals $(j + 1)^{-s}$ if $j + 1$ is squarefree and has an odd number of distinct prime factors, and $0$ otherwise.

results.title: Summability of the odd squarefree terms
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every complex number $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the series of $n^{-s}$ over the squarefree $n \ge 1$ with an odd number of distinct prime factors is summable.

results.title: Sum of $n^{-s}$ over squarefree $n$ with an odd number of prime factors
results.caption: Lemma
results.summary: For every complex number $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the sum of $n^{-s}$ over the squarefree $n \ge 1$ with an odd number of distinct prime factors equals $(\zeta(s)^2 - \zeta(2s))/(2\zeta(s)\zeta(2s))$.

results.title: A discrete subgroup is a lattice iff it has full rank
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space and let $L \subseteq E$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-submodule (an additive subgroup) that is discrete in the subspace topology. results.title: Monsky's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be a finite set of subsets of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ such that every member of $T$ is the convex hull of three points $a, b, c$ of the plane (not necessarily distinct), the union of the members of $T$ is the closed unit square $[0,1]^2$, any two distinct members of $T$ have disjoint interiors, and all members of $T$ have the same Lebesgue measure. Then the number of members of $T$ is even.

results.title: Squaring the square with distinct squares
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There are an integer $n > 1$ and real numbers $x_i$, $y_i$ and $s_i > 0$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$, with the $s_i$ pairwise distinct, such that the union of the closed squares $[x_i, x_i + s_i] \times [y_i, y_i + s_i]$ is the unit square $[0, 1] \times [0, 1]$ and any two of these squares with different indices have disjoint interiors.

results.title: Sylvester–Gallai theorem

results.summary: Every finite non-collinear subset of the real Euclidean plane determines an ordinary line: two points of the set such that no third point of the set is collinear with them.

results.title: Pick's theorem for lattice triangles with a vertex at the origin
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $u, v \in \mathbb{Z}^2$ with $u_0 v_1 - u_1 v_0 \neq 0$, and let $T \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be the convex hull of $0$, $u$ and $v$. Let $I$ be the number of points of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ in the interior of $T$ and $B$ the number of points of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ on the boundary of $T$. Then the area (two-dimensional Lebesgue measure) of $T$ equals $I + B/2 - 1$.

results.title: Pick's theorem for convex lattice polygons
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $V \subset \mathbb{Z}^2$ be a finite set of lattice points, let $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be the convex hull of $V$, and suppose that $P$ has nonempty interior. Let $I$ be the number of points of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ in the interior of $P$ and $B$ the number of points of $\mathbb{Z}^2$ on the boundary of $P$. Then the area (two-dimensional Lebesgue measure) of $P$ equals $I + B/2 - 1$.

results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$ the words $xw$ and $yw$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.

results.title: Syntactic equivalence is compatible with concatenation
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $w, x, y, z \in \Sigma^*$ be words. If $w$ and $x$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, and $y$ and $z$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $wy$ and $xz$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.

results.title: Syntactic congruence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic congruence of $L$ is the monoid congruence on the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that relates words $x$ and $y$ when, for all words $u$ and $v$, $uxv \in L$ if and only if $uyv \in L$.

results.title: Syntactic monoid
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic monoid of $L$ is the quotient of the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ of words by the syntactic congruence of $L$, which relates words $x$ and $y$ when $uxv \in L \iff uyv \in L$ for all words $u$ and $v$.

results.title: Syntactic morphism
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic morphism of $L$ is the monoid homomorphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ of words to the syntactic monoid of $L$ that sends each word to its class under the syntactic congruence of $L$.

results.title: Syntactically equivalent words agree on membership
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then $x \in L$ if and only if $y \in L$.

results.title: Accepting set of the syntactic monoid
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a language $L$, the accepting set of the syntactic monoid of $L$ is the set of syntactic classes of words of $L$: a class belongs to it when its representatives lie in $L$, which does not depend on the representative chosen.

results.title: The syntactic morphism recognizes the language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. For every word $x \in \Sigma^*$, $x \in L$ if and only if the image of $x$ under the syntactic morphism of $L$ lies in the accepting set of the syntactic monoid of $L$, the set of syntactic classes of words of $L$.

results.title: Syntactic equivalence refines Nerode equivalence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$, then they are Nerode equivalent for $L$: the sets $\{z : xz \in L\}$ and $\{z : yz \in L\}$ are equal.

results.title: Equal syntactic classes give equal Nerode classes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language. For all words $x$ and $y$, if the syntactic morphism of $L$ sends $x$ and $y$ to the same element of the syntactic monoid of $L$, then $x$ and $y$ have the same Nerode class with respect to $L$.

results.title: Transition action of a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ and a word $x$, the transition action of $x$ is the map sending each state $q$ of $M$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ starting from $q$.

results.title: Words with the same transition action are syntactically equivalent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $L$ be the language accepted by $M$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ have the same transition action on $M$, that is, for every state $q$, running $M$ from $q$ on $x$ ends in the same state as running $M$ from $q$ on $y$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.

results.title: Syntactically equivalent words act identically
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA that is accessible (every state is reachable from the start state) and state-separated (two states with the same continuation language are equal). If two words $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for the language accepted by $M$, then $x$ and $y$ have the same transition action on $M$: for every state $q$, reading $x$ from $q$ and reading $y$ from $q$ lead to the same state.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$ that is accessible (every state is reached from the start state by some word) and state-separated (distinct states have distinct continuation languages), and let $L$ be the language accepted by $M$. Then two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$ if and only if they have the same transition action on $M$: for every state $q$, running $M$ from $q$ on…

results.title: State transformation monoid
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a type $Q$ of states, the state transformation monoid of $Q$ consists of all functions $Q \to Q$, multiplied by composition in the opposite order: the product $fg$ first applies $f$ and then $g$, so $(fg)(q) = g(f(q))$, and the unit is the identity function.

results.title: State transformations as functions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a type $Q$ of states, the bijection from the state transformations of $Q$ to the functions $Q \to Q$ that sends each transformation to its underlying function; it forgets the multiplication of state transformations.

results.title: Transition transformation of a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ and a word $x$, the transition transformation of $x$ is the transition action of $x$, the map sending each state $q$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ from $q$, regarded as an element of the monoid of state transformations of $M$ (multiplied in reading order: $fg$ applies $f$ first, then $g$).

results.title: Transition morphism of a DFA
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$, the transition morphism is the monoid homomorphism from the free monoid of words to the state transformations of $M$ that sends each word $x$ to its transition action, the map taking each state $q$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ from $q$. State transformations are multiplied in reading order, so the product $fg$ applies $f$ first and then $g$; with this order, the word $xy$ is sent to…

results.title: Transition monoid of a DFA
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The transition monoid of a DFA $M$ is the image of the transition morphism of $M$: the submonoid of state transformations of $M$ consisting of the transition actions of all words, where a word $x$ acts by sending each state $q$ to the state that $M$ reaches by reading $x$ from $q$. State transformations are multiplied in reading order, so the product $fg$ applies $f$ first and then $g$.

results.title: Transition monoid element of a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Each word $x \in \Sigma^*$ determines the element of the transition monoid of $M$ given by the state transformation that sends each state $q$ to the state $M$ reaches from $q$ after reading $x$.

results.title: Syntactic congruence as a kernel
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA and let $L$ be the language $M$ accepts. The syntactic congruence of $L$ equals the kernel of the transition morphism of $M$: two words are syntactically equivalent for $L$ if and only if they induce the same transformation of the states of $M$.

results.title: Action of the syntactic monoid on states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA with state type $Q$, and let $L$ be the language $M$ accepts. This is the monoid homomorphism from the syntactic monoid of $L$ to the state transformation monoid of $Q$ that sends the syntactic class of each word $x$ to the map taking each state $q$ to the state $M$ reaches from $q$ by reading $x$. It is well defined because syntactically equivalent words act…

results.title: Image of the syntactic action
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be an accessible, state-separated DFA and let $L$ be the language $M$ accepts. The image of the action of the syntactic monoid of $L$ on the states of $M$, the monoid homomorphism sending the syntactic class of each word $x$ to the state transformation induced by reading $x$, is exactly the transition monoid of $M$.

results.title: Recognition of a language by a monoid morphism
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$, and let $A \subseteq M$. Then $\varphi$ recognizes $L$ through $A$ when, for every word $w \in \Sigma^*$, $w \in L$ if and only if $\varphi(w) \in A$.

results.title: The syntactic morphism recognizes its language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the syntactic morphism of $L$, from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$, recognizes $L$ through the accepting subset of the syntactic monoid, namely the set of syntactic classes of words in $L$.

results.title: Recognition pulls back along a factorization
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to C$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes $L$ through a subset $A \subseteq C$. If $\varphi = f \circ \psi$ for monoid morphisms $\psi : \Sigma^* \to T$ and $f : T \to C$, then $\psi$ recognizes $L$ through the preimage $f^{-1}(A)$.

results.title: Words with equal recognizer images are syntactically equivalent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on an alphabet $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a set $A \subseteq M$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ satisfy $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$, then $x$ and $y$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$: for all words $u, v \in \Sigma^*$, $uxv \in L$ if and only if $uyv \in L$.

results.title: Recognizer kernels refine the syntactic congruence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a monoid morphism $\varphi$ from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A$ of its codomain, then the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ is contained in the syntactic congruence of $L$: any words $x, y$ with $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$ are syntactically equivalent for $L$.

results.title: Canonical map from a recognizer's kernel quotient to the syntactic monoid
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$, and let $A \subseteq M$ be such that $\varphi$ recognizes $L$ through $A$. Since the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ (words $x, y$ with $\varphi(x) = \varphi(y)$) is contained in the syntactic congruence of $L$, there is a monoid morphism from the quotient of…

results.title: The kernel quotient of a recognizer maps onto the syntactic monoid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a monoid morphism $\varphi$ from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A$ of its codomain, then the canonical monoid morphism from the quotient of $\Sigma^*$ by the kernel congruence of $\varphi$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$, which sends the class of a word $x$ to its syntactic class, is surjective.

results.title: Map from a recognizer's image to the syntactic monoid
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A \subseteq M$. This is the monoid morphism from the image $\varphi(\Sigma^*)$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$ that sends $\varphi(x)$ to the syntactic class of $x$ for every word $x$. It is well defined because words with the same image under $\varphi$ are syntactically…

results.title: The image of a recognizer maps onto the syntactic monoid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A \subseteq M$. Then the canonical monoid morphism from the image $\varphi(\Sigma^*)$ to the syntactic monoid of $L$, which sends $\varphi(x)$ to the syntactic class of $x$, is surjective.

results.title: Finite recognizers give finite syntactic monoids
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to a finite monoid $M$ recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through some subset of $M$, then the syntactic monoid of $L$ is finite.

results.title: Recognition as an inverse image
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$, let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid on $\Sigma$ into a monoid $M$, and let $A \subseteq M$. Then $\varphi$ recognizes $L$ through $A$ if and only if the set of words of $\Sigma^*$ that belong to $L$ equals $\varphi^{-1}(A)$.

results.title: Changing the accepting set off the image of a recognizer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\varphi : \Sigma^* \to M$ be a monoid morphism from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ that recognizes a language $L$ over $\Sigma$ through a subset $A_1 \subseteq M$. If $A_2 \subseteq M$ satisfies $\varphi(x) \in A_1 \iff \varphi(x) \in A_2$ for every word $x$, then $\varphi$ also recognizes $L$ through $A_2$.

results.title: The syntactic DFA
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. The syntactic DFA of $L$ has the syntactic monoid of $L$ as its set of states, the identity $1$ as start state, and the syntactic classes of the words of $L$ as accepting states; from a state $q$, reading a letter $a \in \Sigma$ leads to $q \cdot [a]$, where $[a]$ is the syntactic class of the one-letter word $a$.

results.title: Runs of the syntactic DFA
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. For every state $q$ of the syntactic DFA of $L$ (an element of the syntactic monoid of $L$) and every word $x \in \Sigma^*$, the state reached from $q$ by reading $x$ is $q \cdot [x]$, where $[x]$ is the image of $x$ under the syntactic morphism of $L$.

results.title: The syntactic DFA accepts its language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every language $L$, the syntactic DFA of $L$ accepts exactly $L$.

results.title: The syntactic DFA is accessible
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every language $L$, every state of the syntactic DFA of $L$ is reachable: some word leads to it from the start state.

results.title: Finite syntactic monoid implies regularity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every language whose syntactic monoid is finite is regular.

results.title: The syntactic DFA of a language with finite syntactic monoid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the syntactic monoid of a language $L$ is finite, then the syntactic DFA of $L$ has finitely many states and accepts exactly $L$.

results.title: The transition morphism of a DFA recognizes its language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA over an alphabet $\Sigma$ with state set $Q$, start state $q_0$ and set of accepting states $F$. The transition morphism of $M$, from the free monoid $\Sigma^*$ to the monoid of state transformations of $Q$, recognizes the language accepted by $M$ through the set of transformations $f$ with $f(q_0) \in F$.

results.title: Languages of finite automata have finite syntactic monoids
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every language accepted by a DFA with finitely many states has a finite syntactic monoid.
